text: 8 Combustion occurs when fuel and oxygen react to produce carbon dioxide, water and heat. For the foreseeable future, the overwhelming majority of delivered energy in terrestrial applications will be from combustion or other chemically reacting systems. These energy uses cover the range from electric power and transportation to processes directly tied to the delivered material (e.g., glass and steel manufacture). These processes produce some of the most important environmental hazards currently facing humanity (global climate change, acid gas pollution, mercury contamination from coal, and wild-land fires). Despite being the subject of active research for over 80 years, combustion processes remain one of the most poorly controlled phenomena that have a significant impact on human health,

source: NASA ISS Researcher's Guide: Combustion Science (NP-2015-10-034-JSC)
text: combustion processes remain one of the most poorly controlled phenomena that have a significant impact on human health, comfort and safety. This is because the simplest combustor (e.g., kitchen stove) remains beyond our detailed numerical modeling capabilities. Typically, the combustion process involves a large number of chemical species (hundreds) and reactions (even thousands). It is these species and reactions that determine flammability limits (combustor operating ranges) and pollutant emissions. Much of combustion research involves developing a comprehensive and predictive quantitative understanding of this complex process. This understanding usually occurs in smaller, bench-scale experiments that are amenable to detailed study and modeling. In these bench-scale experiments, however,

In these bench-scale experiments, however, buoyant forces, created by gravity and the large temperature differential between the flame and the ambient gas, dominate and frequently obscure the physical and chemical phenomena of interest, and hence, complicate analyses. In the absence of gravity, buoyancy can be suppressed, and the analyses can be reduced to much simpler one- dimensional systems. To understand the strong influence of gravity on flames, one can consider the density gradients in flames. Typical flame temperatures are on the order of 2,300 degrees Kelvin, whereas ambient temperatures are approximately 300 degrees Kelvin. This produces an eight-fold density change over the scale of a centimeter. The

The resultant density gradient induces a strong velocity field that dominates all but the highest flow fields. This flow field causes the flame to lift and point upward. The resultant flow instabilities cause the flicker typical of flames on Earth. Figure 1 contains a gallery of 1-g to 0-g comparison flames. By varying or eliminating the effects of gravity, we can extract fundamental data that are important for understanding combustion systems. This approach has been implemented to some extent in existing terrestrial reduced-gravity platforms, but the experimental time scales and sizes have been limited. Fire safety is an important operational element of human space exploration missions to minimize the likelihood and impact of accidental fires in spacecraft and human habitats. Overall improvements were made in the ability to model droplet combustion in spray combustors (e.g., jet engines), predict flame spread, predict soot production, and detection and prevention of spacecraft fires. text: 16 Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) Research, especially including that already conducted in microgravity, has revealed that our current predictive ability is significantly lacking for flames at the extremes of fuel dilution, namely for sooty, pure-fuel flames and dilute flames that are near extinction. The general goal of the CLD Flame experiment is to extend the range of flame conditions that can be accurately predicted by developing and experimentally verifying chemical kinetic and soot formation submodels. The dependence of normal coflow flames on injection velocity and fuel dilution will be carefully examined for flames at both very dilute and highly sooting conditions. Measurements will be made of the structure of diluted methane and ethylene flames in an air coflow.

Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) Electric fields can strongly influence flames because of their effect on the ions present as a result of the combustion reactions. The direct ion transport and the induced ion wind can modify the flame shape, alter the soot or flammability limits, direct heat transfer, and reduce pollutant emission. Tests will be conducted with various concentrations of both the injected fuel (i.e., ethylene or methane) and the oxygen-enriched atmosphere in order to determine the role of the flame structure on soot inception (Figure 6). Flame Existence One of the most seemingly simple, but long-standing, questions addressed by microgravity testing involved whether flames could even exist without buoyancy. Many researchers, including notable experts, argued openly in the scientific literature that, in the absence of convection, a steady flame could not exist; diffusive transport alone could not sustain a flame. Two spaceflight experiments demonstrated conclusively the fallacy of such arguments. The first involved the behavior of a simple candle flame in a long-duration microgravity environment (Dietrich et al., 2000). text: Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX). Objective: Study heptane and methanol droplets in O2/N2 mixtures diluted with a second inert gas (nitrogen, carbon dioxide, helium or xenon) to see how an inert suppressant changes the flammability limit of the two fuels. What varied: Ambient O2, inert diluent type and amount, pressure, droplet size. Key result: The flammability limit is lower in reduced gravity; the limiting oxygen index (LOI) is significantly lower than in normal gravity and lower than predicted. Stable cool flames form after radiative extinction of heptane droplets. Fire-safety implication: Terrestrial standards for inert-gas suppressants do not offer the same margin of safety in low gravity as in normal gravity.

text: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS). Objective: Examine burning and extinction of a wide variety of solid fuel samples in microgravity, to improve 1-g material fire-safety tests and guide extinguishing strategies. What varied: Airflow speed (main variable), oxygen (nitrogen dilution), nitrogen suppressant jet. Key result: NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 is not conservative: materials can burn at lower oxygen in microgravity than on Earth. Local suppressant application was not adequate; the jet entrained air and sustained the flame, and nitrogen could even strengthen it. Fire-safety implication: Materials screened as safe in 1-g may burn in a spacecraft; extinguisher placement needs rethinking because a suppressant jet can feed a microgravity flame.

text: Water Mist Fire Suppression (Mist). Objective: Measure how water droplet diameter and water concentration affect the speed, strength and shape of premixed flames, to design better mist suppression systems replacing Halon. What varied: Water droplet diameter, water concentration, fuel and oxygen mixture. Key result: Led to non-toxic water-mist portable fire extinguishers certified for spaceflight; the first two of nine reached the ISS in December 2015 to replace CO2 units. Fire-safety implication: Direct path from microgravity research to a crew fire-suppression tool.

source: NASA ISS Researcher's Guide: Combustion Science (NP-2015-10-034-JSC), p. 26, 35, 45
text: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME). Objective: Measure the particle-size distribution of smoke from spacecraft materials. What varied: Spacecraft material. Key result: Microgravity flames produce very different particulate sizes, so detectors that sense particulates need different signatures in space. Fire-safety implication: Guidance for designers of future spacecraft smoke detectors.

source: NASA ISS Researcher's Guide: Combustion Science (NP-2015-10-034-JSC); Dietrich et al. (2000), p. 9, 30, 33
text: Candle Flames (Mir). Objective: Observe a candle flame in long-duration microgravity aboard Mir. Key result: Microgravity candle flames burned over 45 minutes, to a lower ambient oxygen than an identical candle on Earth, and oscillated before extinction. Fire-safety implication: Refutes the belief that a steady fire cannot exist in quiescent microgravity.

source: NASA ISS Researcher's Guide: Combustion Science (NP-2015-10-034-JSC), p. 33-34, 41-42
text: Cool Flames (CIR initiative). Objective: Find the pre-conditions for hot-flame/cool-flame transitions, cool-flame stability and spontaneous re-ignition, using existing FLEX-2 MDCA hardware. What varied: Fuel type, pressure, diluent concentration. Key result: Builds on FLEX: after hot-flame extinction, heptane droplets kept burning with a low-temperature cool flame. Fire-safety implication: Very weak, persistent flames invisible to the eye can spontaneously re-ignite long after the visible flame is gone.

source: PSI-159

source: Fire-Margin analysis of PSI-69 FLEX table (DOI 10.60555/mbq8-0451)
text: High oxygen turns droplet burns into bursts. Objective: Compare how FLEX droplet tests ended at high vs air-level oxygen. What varied: Ambient O2 (all fuels, diluents and pressures pooled). Key result: At O2 >= 0.25, 24 of 30 tests ended in Disruption (80%); at O2 <= 0.21, 22 of 206 (10.7%). Fire-safety implication: In an oxygen-enriched habitat a burning droplet is more likely to burst and scatter fuel than to burn out quietly. Cells are small and pressure coverage is uneven, so treat this as a strong signal, not a law.

source: Fire-Margin analysis of PSI-69 FLEX table (DOI 10.60555/mbq8-0451); PSI-25; PSI-159; Urban et al., Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment, ICES-2024-365; test matrix in NTRS 20240007488 presentation
text: Where Moon-base fire evidence exists, and where it does not. Objective: Check whether real tests reach the 34% O2 / 8.2 psia (0.558 atm) habitat atmosphere. What varied: Fuel type; PSI public data vs verified literature. Key result: In PSI's public data, solid materials stop at 22.2% O2. Only 3 solid samples (Saffire-VI, 2024) burned near Moon-base conditions (29%-31% O2, ~0.54 atm): not in PSI, one flight, no partial gravity. Gas flames (CFI-G) were tested at 33%-39% O2 / 0.50 atm; FLEX droplets reach 34% O2 but only at >= 0.69 atm, and at O2 >= 25% 80% of FLEX tests ended in Disruption. Fire-safety implication: Cabin-material and droplet fire behaviour at the planned habitat atmosphere rests on one literature flight: the next experiments should target that corner, including partial gravity.

source: Fire-Margin analysis of PSI-69 FLEX table (DOI 10.60555/mbq8-0451); models/metrics.json
text: The d-squared law only fits droplets that burn out. Objective: Check burn time against the d-squared law t = d0^2 / K. What varied: Test outcome (Completion vs early end). Key result: For Completion tests, d0^2/Ktracks measured burn time (r = 0.92, n = 27); across all tests r = 0.16 because extinction or disruption ends the burn early. Fire-safety implication: Use d0^2/Kas an upper limit on burn time, never as a prediction for droplets that may extinguish or burst.

source: NASA ISS Researcher's Guide: Combustion Science (NP-2015-10-034-JSC), p. 35
text: Three misconceptions about spacecraft fire. Objective: Misconceptions that shaped early spacecraft fire safety. Key result: (1) Asteady fire cannot exist in a quiescent microgravity environment. (2) Afire will self-extinguish if ventilation is shut off. (3) Because the reduced-gravity environment is inherently safer, terrestrial fire standards and tests represent a very conservative approach to fire safety. Fire-safety implication: Research at NASA GRC and in microgravity showed all three are false.

source: Olson et al., ICES 2019, 'Flammability Limits from BASS-II Testing in Microgravity Compared to Normal Gravity Limits'
text: BASS-II: lower-oxygen burning in micro-g. Key result: Materials burn at lower oxygen concentrations in microgravity than in normal gravity. Fire-safety implication: Shutting down ventilation may not extinguish flames in high-oxygen, low-pressure exploration atmospheres.

source: NASA Apollo 204 Review Board findings; NASA news release 'Fifty Years On, Apollo 1 Tragedy Offers Vital Lessons'; NASA ISS Researcher's Guide: Combustion Science (NP-2015-10-034-JSC) p. 34
text: Apollo 1 cabin fire (1967). During a launch-pad test the cabin was filled with high-pressure 100% oxygen; a spark from an electrical short ignited flammable cabin material. Three astronauts died. Lesson: Oxygen-rich cabins turn ordinary materials into fuel: NASA changed the spacecraft (Block II), cabin materials and hatch, and designed fire-resistant spacesuits.

source: NASA, '50 Years Ago: Apollo 13 Review Board Report'; NASA ISS Researcher's Guide: Combustion Science (NP-2015-10-034-JSC) p. 34
text: Apollo 13 oxygen tank explosion (1970). Wires damaged during pre-flight testing shorted inside oxygen tank no. 2 when the fans were switched on; the Teflon insulation burned, pressure rose and the tank ruptured. Lesson: Ignition sources inside pure-oxygen systems are a fire hazard even far from the cabin.

source: NASA, '25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir'
text: Mir oxygen-generator fire (1997). On 23 February 1997 a solid-fuel oxygen generator ('candle') in Kvant-1 burned with a blowtorch-like flame; the crew put it out with water-based foam extinguishers. Lesson: Oxygen sources themselves can be fire sources; suppression in microgravity must reach a flame that does not behave like one on Earth.

source: NASA Spinoff, 'Fireman's Air Tanks'
text: Lighter firefighter air tanks. NASA work on lightweight composite pressure vessels led to firefighter breathing-air tanks with an aluminum liner wrapped in resin-impregnated glass fiber. Lesson: Lighter tanks mean less strain on firefighters carrying their own air supply.

source: NASA ISS Researcher's Guide: Combustion Science (NP-2015-10-034-JSC) p. 35
text: Smarter fire detector. Microgravity research showed fire particulates differ in space. NASA Glenn built a device that monitors particulates and chemical species together; in FAA testing it beat aircraft smoke detectors at rejecting false alarms and detecting real events. Lesson: Detecting fire by what it really emits, not by Earth-based assumptions.

source: NASA Spinoff 2008, 'Polymer Fabric Protects Firefighters, Military, and Civilians'
text: Fire-resistant fabric (PBI). NASA helped develop PBI, a heat- and flame-resistant fiber now used in firefighting, military and motor-sport gear. Lesson: Materials born from post-Apollo-1 fire safety protect firefighters on Earth.
